full_judgment:
4. The respondent filed case, being No. 17 of 1987 (Kha 14, Lalmatia, Mohammadpur) seeking release of the property before the Court of Settlement as per provision of section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 averring the facts as stated hereinabove. 

 5. The appellant No. 1 contested the case before the Court of Settlement contending, amongst others, that listing of the property in the Kha list is guide legal. It was the specific case of the appellant No. 1 that after liberation of the country whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan, the owner of the property were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh and thereupon the property having had assumed the character of the abandoned property the same has legally been listed in the list of abandoned buildings. It was also the contention of the appellant No. 1 before the Court of Settlement that the agreement for sale claimed to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan is not genuine and that the agreement for sale is a fabricated one and that the same has been brought into existence only to grab the property. 

 6. It may be mentioned section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 requires the claimant of the property, who has filed petition before the Court of Settlement seeking exclusion of the property from the list of abandoned buildings, or to return the same to him or contending that the building is not an abandoned property and has not vested in the Government and that his right and interest in the building has not been affected by the provision of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, is to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property. So, it is seen from the provision of section 7 of the Ordinance that onus of establishing that the inclusion of the building, i.e. exclusion whereof from the list of abandoned properties has been sought for by a claimant of the building, in the list of abandoned building is not legal is on the claimant and he is to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property. 

 7. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the respondent herein before the said Court based his claim in the property in question on the basis of the ex parte decree obtained in the suit filed seeking specific performance of contract for sale of land said to have been entered into between the respondent and Mr SM Hasan, the owner of the property on the basis of lease from the Government of the then East Pakistan. It is also seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court directed the respondent to file the deed of agreement said to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan and the lease deed on the basis whereof Mr SM Hasan got the property in question. Although the respondent took time to produce the said documents but ultimately did not produce the said documents before the Court of Settlement. It seems the Court of Settlement in the background of the contentions of the appellant No. 1 who was opposite party before the Court of Settlement, that the agreement for sale said to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan was not genuine and that Mr SM Hasan after emergence of Bangladesh was not in Bangladesh and that when PO 16 of 1972 came into force whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan, prior to that and after that, were not known, directed the respondent to produce the said documents to ascertain the genuineness of the agreement for sale claimed to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan on August 1, 1973. 

 8. It may be mentioned the Court of Settlement when it finally took up the case for hearing on the date fixed neither the respondent nor his lawyer was present. The Court of Settlement dismissed the case on the finding "From the papers submitted before us by the parties and in the absence of original agreement for sale and that other evidence on the point it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner." 

 10. As against the judgment of the Court of Settlement the respondent moved the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division on the findings and observations that the Court of Settlement disregarded the ex parte decree and also the kabala in favour of the petitioner (herein respondent) on the ground that he was not able to furnish the deed of agreement which was the basis of the ex parte decree and the kabala, and that the Court of Settlement did not refer to any other aspect of the case, that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the Kha list as required by section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, that as per provision of Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 the Government is required to serve a notice if it intends to take possession of the building which has been considered as abandoned building or abandoned property, that in case of noncompliance with the notice served under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 the Government is required to proceed as per provision of Article 7(4) of PO 16 of 1972, that as no notice under section 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served thereby the petitioner was deprived of valuable right to approach the appropriate authority as per provision of the said PO 16 of 1972 for the redress of his grievance as regard treating the property as abandoned and, as such, non service of notice under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 "has itself rendered the inclusion of the property in question in the Kha list illegal", that the Court of Settlement went beyond its jurisdiction in dismissing the case upon ignoring the ex parte decree and later on the kabala executed through the Court in favour of the petitioner and that in ignoring the said decree and kabala the Court of fact, in fact, made those nugatory, that as per provision of section 7 of the Ordinance of 1985 the Court of Settlement is limited to the consideration of right or interest of the claimant of the property and examination of title or questioning the same is not within the jurisdiction of the said Court, that the Court of Settlement is not authorised to adjudicate the title of the claimant, particularly when there is a decree of the civil Court, that jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement is primarily limited to the inquiry whether the property is an abandoned property and that in the presence of a decree of the civil Court the Court of Settlement which has been established for a specific purpose is not authorized to give a contrary finding as to the title of the party, that the Court of Settlement was in error in not giving any finding whether the notice under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served upon the petitioner and that the Court of Settlement only because of the absence of the deed of agreement and the original lease deed was in error in holding that the ex parte decree and the kabala were fraudulent, that no notice was served on the petitioner before listing the property. The High Court Division finally observing "thus we are in a position to say that the Court of Settlement was not authorised to nullify the decree obtained from the Civil Court and the kabala in favour of the petitioner only on the ground that the petitioner was not able to file the original deed of agreement" made the Rule absolute upon setting aside the order of the Court of Settlement and thereupon declared that the property in question is not an abandoned property. 

 11. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the Court of Settlement was wrong in not excluding the property in question from the list of abandoned property in view of the decree of specific performance obtained by the writ petitioner-respondent and that the High Court Division was wrong in assuming that non-service of notice in treating the property as abandoned property is an admitted fact and holding that in the absence of service of notice the property cannot be treated as an abandoned property. 

 12. It may be mentioned the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute has observed "in the instant case it is not disputed that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the `Kha' list, and therefore want of notice from the Government to the petitioner under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 has itself rendered the inclusion of the property in question in the 'Kha' list illegal. Therefore, we hold that the Settlement Court erred in not giving any finding whether the notice upon the petitioner under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served upon the petitioner. We find that no notice was actually served". 

 14. In our view in the background of the aforesaid assertion of the respondent i.e. appellant No. 1, the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that non service of notice prior to the listing of the property is an undisputed one. We are of the view that the High Court Division was in error in holding that no notice was served prior to the listing of the property since the writ petitioner did not place any material before the Court of Settlement in support of his contention that in listing the property as abandoned property no notice was served. The petitioner did not lead any evidence to substantiate his contention as to non service of notice since it is not seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that any such contention was raised and the respondent made attempt to establish his claim of non-service of notice in listing the property as abandoned property. It may be mentioned because of the provision of sections 5(2) and 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 whatever facts are asserted by the petitioner before the Court of Settlement in support of his claim to the property listed as abandoned, it is he who is to establish the same and thereupon onus to rebut the said fact is on the authority that listed the property as abandoned property. 

 15. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that it has taken serious exception as regard the judgment of the Court of Settlement in dismissing the petition filed by the respondent under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for not taking into consideration the ex parte decree in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land and the kabala obtained in execution of the said decree as regard the property in question. In the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 it has been held that a decree in suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land is not a bar for listing a building as abandoned building. This being the position the listing of the building in question as abandoned property was quite legal. Provision of section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 enjoins upon the claimant of the property, which has been listed as abandoned property, in view of the provision of section 5(2) of the Ordinance, to establish that the building listed as abandoned is not an abandoned property. From the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is seen that the respondent miserably failed to establish before the said Court that the building in question is not an abandoned property. 

 16. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute and thereupon declaring that property in question is not an abandoned property held that the Court of Settlement was in error in not taking into notice the ex parte decree in the suit for specific performance of the contract for sale of building in question and the kabala obtained on the basis of the said ex parte decree and thereupon dismissing the case filed under section 7(1) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. Suffice it to say that as per provision of section 5 of the Ordinance the decree of the kind obtained by the writ petitioner was not a bar in listing the property in question as abandoned building as has been held by this Division in the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71. On going through the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division proceeded on the premise that the Court of Settlement was in error in ignoring the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract and the kabala obtained on the basis thereof but the same was not a legally well founded premises because of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court in disposing of the case did not enter into the question of title of the respondent, rather proceeded to ascertain the fact whether at the relevant time, in the background of the contention of the appellant before the Court of Settlement that after emergence of Bangladesh whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh either before or after the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 the owner of the property was in Bangladesh when PO 16 of 1972 was promulgated. To ascertain the genuineness of the agreement for sale, since presence of the owner of the property in Bangladesh at the relevant time was assertively challenged by the abandoned property authority, the respondent was directed by the Court of Settlement to produce the same but the respondent did not produce the said agreement for sale. Undoubtedly, the Court of Settlement was within its jurisdiction in directing the respondent to produce the agreement and the lease deed before the said Court for the purpose of making decision on the question as to whether at the relevant time whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan were known and that he was in Bangladesh. Since those facts are in the negative i.e. Mr SM Hasan's whereabouts were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh after emergence of Bangladesh, and, as such, undoubtedly the property in question on the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 assumed the character of abandoned building and in that background of the fact the property was legally listed in the list of abandoned buildings. 

 17. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that the Court of Settlement in disposing of the case did not give adequate opportunity to the respondent to place his case. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondent that the Court of Settlement in not allowing the respondent to place evidence and thus having had shut out the opportunity of producing evidence for proper adjudication of the case, as such, the High Court Division was quite correct in setting aside the judgment of the Court of Settlement. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that opportunity was given to the respondent to produce the materials required by the Court but he failed to do that and in that background of the fact of the case the Court of Settlement dismissed the case against him. From the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is seen that the evidence which was required to be produced by the respondent for adjudication of the case, he having had not produced the same the Court dismissed the case upon observing that in the absence of the said material and oral evidence "it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner" and further observing "the petitioner has not been able to establish his case as asked for". This being the position the submission of the learned Counsel for the respondent that the Court of Settlement decided the case on shutting out the evidence by way of depriving the respondent from producing evidence is not well conceived one. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that in view of the provision of section 10(5) of the Ordinance the Court of Settlement was required to decide the case on merit on the basis of evidence on record but the said Court having had not done so the judgment of the said Court has rightly been set aside by the High Court Division. This submission is not correct. Since it is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court on consideration of the materials brought on record from the side of the respondent and default made by him in not producing the material directed by the Court, the Court dismissed the case on the finding that the respondent failed to prove his case and the Court had observed in the background of the materials on record "it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner". 

 18. In the background of the proposition of law laid down by this Division a decree in a suit for specific conformance of contract and a kabala obtained on the basis thereof is no bar in listing a property in the list of abandoned building. Because of the provisions of section 5(2) and section 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 it was incumbent upon the respondent to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property and that the said onus having not been discharged by the respondent or in other words, it having not been established by the respondent that the property in question is not an abandoned property and that it having not been established by the respondent that at the relevant time whereabouts of the owner of the property were very much known as he was very much present in Bangladesh and was managing the property in question the High Court Division was in error in setting aside the judgment of the Court of Settlement. The respondent had also not established his contention that no notice was served in listing the abandoned building. The High Court Division as already mentioned proceeded on the premises that "it is not disputed that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the Kha list" although it was the definite assertion of the writ respondent i.e. the appellant, that notice under the provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was duly issued and served before listing the property in question in the list of abandoned buildings. 

 21. In the instant case the High Court Division, in fact, in spite of the absence of any one of situations stated hereinbefore on fresh assessment of the materials and placing reliance on the materials which under the law could only have been the materials for consideration by the Court of Settlement, but in spite of having the opportunity respondent withheld the said materials, had the same been filed before it in deciding the question whether the property is an abandoned property and the respondent is entitled to get the property released from the list of abandoned buildings came to a different finding and thereupon substituted the said finding for the finding of the Court of Settlement and then made the Rule absolute.
